tracks.title: Python foundations
tracks.description: Read small pieces of code and explore variables, loops and functions.

questions.statement: After price = 10 and quantity = 3, price * quantity evaluates to 30.
questions.feedback: Python uses * for multiplication. Multiplying the two stored numbers gives 30.

questions.statement: In Python, "5" + "2" evaluates to the number 7.
questions.feedback: Quotation marks make these strings. The + operator joins them into "52". Convert them to numbers to add them.
Python list indexing starts at zero, so index 0 selects the first item.

questions.statement: The loop for n in range(3): visits the values 1, 2 and 3.
questions.feedback: range(3) produces 0, 1 and 2. The stop value is excluded.

questions.statement: A Python function can return a result to the code that called it.
questions.feedback: return passes a value back to the caller. Printing a value only displays it; these are different actions.

questions.statement: After first = [1, 2]; second = first; second.append(3), first still contains only [1, 2].
questions.feedback: Both names refer to the same list here, so appending through second also changes what first refers to. A separate list copy avoids this shared change.

tracks.title: AI at work
tracks.description: Try everyday decisions about prompts, checking answers and responsible use.

questions.statement: An AI-generated answer should be checked before using it for an important business decision.
questions.feedback: A confident answer can still be wrong. Check important claims against reliable sources and involve the appropriate people.

questions.statement: A detailed prompt guarantees that an AI answer will be factually correct.
questions.feedback: Context and clear instructions can improve an answer, but cannot guarantee its accuracy. Verification still matters.

questions.statement: You should check your organisation’s approved tools and data rules before entering confidential customer information into an AI service.
questions.feedback: Use an approved tool and the organisation’s agreed data-handling process. Do not assume every service has the same settings or terms.

questions.statement: A useful prompt can specify the audience, goal and desired output format.
questions.feedback: These details give the model useful context. Add relevant approved information, then review the result against the task.

questions.statement: Retrieval-augmented generation means the model automatically retrains its weights whenever a new document is added.
questions.feedback: RAG retrieves information and supplies it as context for generation. It does not, by itself, retrain model weights.

questions.statement: If an AI-generated email sounds convincing, it can safely promise a customer a discount without checking company policy.
questions.feedback: Commercial promises need approved facts and the required staff authority. Persuasive wording is not permission to offer a discount.

tracks.title: Excel and data basics
tracks.description: Check formulas, references and everyday data-handling choices.

questions.statement: A standard Excel formula begins with an equals sign (=).
questions.feedback: The equals sign tells Excel to calculate an expression, such as =A1+B1.

questions.statement: =SUM(A1:A3) adds the values in A1, A2 and A3.
questions.feedback: The colon describes a range, and SUM adds the numeric values in it.

questions.statement: Sorting just one column of a customer table can separate names from their matching contact details.
questions.feedback: Keep related rows together when sorting. Select the whole related table or use the table’s sort controls.

questions.statement: If =A1 is copied one column to the right, the relative reference remains A1.
questions.feedback: A relative reference moves with the copied formula, so it becomes B1 in this example.

questions.statement: The reference $A$1 fixes both the column and row when a formula is copied.
questions.feedback: The dollar signs make the column and row absolute references. This helps when many calculations use one fixed input.

questions.statement: An average alone is always enough to understand a dataset, even if a few values are much larger than the rest.
questions.feedback: Large outliers can move the average. Look at the distribution, median, missing values and business context as appropriate.
